Q: Calculate multiple stats for two or more columns in R data.table A:

By total coincidence I was working today on a helper function calls_across that does exactly what you want. It pairs with the env programming mechanism in recent versions of {data.table}.

[Edit: as promised, now allowing aliasing the functions on the fly via a named character vector (which preserves GForce)]

library(data.table)
set.seed(1) # please use a seed for reproducibility!!!
dt <- data.table(class = rep(letters[1:3], 4), val1=sample(12), val2=sample(12)*10)

query <- calls_across(
  c(maximo="max", minimo="min"),
  c("val1", "val2"),
  na.rm=TRUE,
  order="col_fun"
)

dt[, j, by=class, env=list(j=query)]
#>     class val1_maximo val1_minimo val2_maximo val2_minimo
#>    <char>       <int>       <int>       <num>       <num>
#> 1:      a          11           1         120          40
#> 2:      b          12           2         110          10
#> 3:      c          10           5          90          30

Output with verbose=TRUE:

dt[, j, by=class, env=list(j=query), verbose=TRUE]
#> Argument 'by' after substitute: class
#> Argument 'j' after substitute: list(val1_maximo = max(val1, na.rm = TRUE), val1_minimo = min(val1, na.rm = TRUE), val2_maximo = max(val2, na.rm = TRUE), val2_minimo = min(val2, na.rm = TRUE))
#> [...]
#> GForce optimized j to 'list(gmax(val1, na.rm = TRUE), gmin(val1, na.rm = TRUE), gmax(val2, na.rm = TRUE), gmin(val2, na.rm = TRUE))' (see ?GForce)
#> Making each group and running j (GForce TRUE) ...
#> [...]

Note: {data.table}'s "GForce" optimisations of common stats functions avoid (slow) split-apply-combine when there is a by, so it's important to take advantage of them.

I will change the code to allow such aliasing in the funs argument (using a named character vector). (Let me do that later and edit at some point.)[done]

Here is the source code, still a bit WIP [but now revised to allow optional aliases]:

calls_across <- function(
    funs,
    cols,
    ...,
    order  = c("fun_col","col_fun"),
    named  = TRUE,
    naming = order,
    sep    = "_"
){
  order <- match.arg(order)
  stopifnot(naming %in% c("fun_col","col_fun"))
  .make_call <- function(fun, col, ...) {
    dots <- as.list(substitute(list(...)))[-1]
    as.call(c(list(as.name(fun), as.name(col)), dots))
  }
  if (isTRUE(named)) fun_nms <- if (!is.null(names(funs))) names(funs) else funs
  if (match.arg(order)=="fun_col") {
    ans <- lapply(funs, \(f) lapply(cols, \(c) .make_call(f,c,...)))
    if (isTRUE(named)) {
      .f <- rep(fun_nms, each=length(cols))
      .c <- rep(cols,times=length(funs))
    }
  } else {
    ans <- lapply(cols, \(c) lapply(funs, \(f) .make_call(f,c,...)))
    if (isTRUE(named)) {
      .f <- rep(fun_nms, times=length(cols))
      .c <- rep(cols, each=length(funs))
    }
  }
  ans <- do.call(c, ans)
  if (isTRUE(named)) names(ans) <- if (naming=="fun_col") paste(.f,.c,sep=sep) else paste(.c,.f,sep=sep)
  ans
}

It allows separate flexibility over i) the order and ii) the names of the output columns (fun-then-col or col-then-fun). Please notice from the examples that it also permits additional arguments, such as na.rm=TRUE.

Q: IntelliJ or EclipseIDE. Which is better? A:

As mentioned already by others, it is a matter of choice and at the end, you should use what works better.
Some people prefer IntelliJ, some prefer Eclipse. Both IDEs are really good and powerful.

I personally prefer using the Eclipse IDE for quite a few reasons, some more important than others. This post/reply/answer/whatever Stack Overflow calls it shows these reasons (but is not necessarily exhaustive).

But before comparing them, you should be aware of one important difference: While all (official) Eclipse IDE products are free and Open Source, IntelliJ comes with the Community Edition (mostly Open Source) and an Ultimate Edition (paid), even though both use the same binary/installer nowadays. If you want to compare them in some way, please first think about which edition of IntelliJ (Community Edition vs Ultimate Edition) you are comparing to which Eclipse product (e.g. Eclipse IDE for Java Developers and Eclipse IDE for Enterprise Java and Web Developers).

Application differences

Debugging

I prefer how debugging Java applications works in Eclipse. One of the reasons for this is that Eclipse shows me the returned value of a method after it has been called. I often rely on that feature, especially when the result of a method call is not assigned to a variable.

In addition to that, using "Hot Code Replace" just works with Eclipse without me setting up anything or needing to use any additional key combinations. I edit the code, save the Java file and it automatically replaces the code without needing to restart the application, even in a method that is currently executed/that I'm stepping through. While this also works in IntelliJ, I feel like it's more complicated to get working and I have to remember the additional key combination for building the project.

Platform, plugins

The "core" of the Eclipse IDE is Eclipse Platform which provides a really powerful framework for building applications like the Eclipse IDEs (providing the workspace model, editors, common views and many other basic building blocks). This is far more powerful and extensible than IntelliJ or anything comparable to it. People are not just building plugins on top of the Eclipse IDE, companies are building fully-fledged products on top of Eclipse Platform (these are called Eclipse RCP apps).

Similar to IntelliJ (which has variants for different programming languages like CLion or PHPStorm), Eclipse comes in many variants called packages or products (see this page). However, in contrast to IntelliJ, the Eclipse IDE gives me more power when I want to create a custom installation with what I want. I can start with one package and continue installing and removing what I want. I can start with a minimal Eclipse Platform installation and only install the plugins I want to use (e.g. only the standard Java tooling with debugging support and Maven if I want this).

Lightweight

This also brings me to the fact that Eclipse can be more lightweight than IntelliJ. In my experience, Eclipse (let's say the default Eclipse IDE for Java Developers) works way better on constrained machines or when you want it to not consume a lot of resources. This is especially the case if you want to work on many projects together in the same workspace (as opposed to opening each project in dedicated IntelliJ windows). However, if you add a lot of plugins or have a lot of projects you don't use in your workspace, you can obviously lose this.

If you really want to, you could create a minimal Eclipse installation with Java tooling that runs with a heap size of just 256MB.

DBeaver

While IntelliJ Ultimate Edition/DataGrip includes a tool for working with databases (I think that's only available in the paid version but it's possible that this changed), I really like DBeaver which is a standalong Eclipse RCP application (Note that DBeaver is not an Eclipse project under the Umbrella of the Eclipse Foundation). And because it is an Eclipse-based application, I can just install it in my existing Eclipse installation and have all the functionality available to me right in my IDE. This is also possible with many other Eclipse-based tools like Eclipse Memory Analyzer or IBM MQ Explorer (commercial) (but finding an Update site to install these tools can be difficult).

Workspace-based

The Eclipse IDE is a workspace-based IDE while IntelliJ is project-based. In Eclipse, I have a workspace that has as many (possibly but not necessarily related) projects as I like. I can also organize my projects into working sets if I want to group multiple projects together.

With Maven, having multiple projects in the same Eclipse workspace means that they are linked together automatically if they depend on another (if the artifact coordinates match). If project A depends on project B and I change something in project B, these changes are applied immediately to project A because Eclipse recognizes the dependency. This is really useful when working with multiple projects depending on each other.

At work, I am using one workspace with many related projects. I group them into working sets (with those being configured as the top level elements in the package explorer) and I can expand/collapse them as needed. Using different windows for all of the projects I'm working on (especially when making some change affecting many of these projects) would just be a nightmare.

Layout and perspectives

Eclipse gives me the option to move and customize the layout as I like and save it into perspectives (e.g. there's one for Java Development and one for Debugging) with different layouts. Some of these customizations (and especially the concept of perspectives) aren't as easy to do with IntelliJ.

Configurability

In my experience, Eclipse is much more configurable than IntelliJ. There are many, many options where I can configure Eclipse's behavior. This affects the installation itself (as mentioned before, I can create an Eclipse installation containing whatever I like), preferences (both for a workspace and per-project), the layout (e.g. toolbars) and other things.

Indexing

In the past, I faced some issues with indexing projects with IntelliJ. When opening a project in IntelliJ, it needs to index everything (which can take quite a lot of time) and it is kind of unusable before it's finished with that (it's possible that this got better). With the Eclipse IDE, I don't need to worry about indexing.

Hidden features

With Eclipse being there for long time, there are a lot of features in Eclipse, many of them disabled by default or somewhat hidden. One example of that is the ability to open different parts of the same file in two editors with Eclipse automatically updating the other editor. I can open the same Java file in two editors but configure the editors to only show specific Java elements (e.g. different nested classes), update those parts and Eclipse keeps them synchronized with each other.

Maven

Maven is one of the build tools you would use in Java and I really like Eclipse's Maven support.
While I mostly edit pom.xml files as text, the POM editor is really useful and quite powerful.

For instance, it has Dependencies and Dependency Hierarchy tabs that provide a GUI that allows displaying dependencies (including transitive dependencies and where they are coming from) as well as editing the dependencies of my projects. It also comes with an Effective POM tab that shows the actual merged ("effective") POM content containing all configurations of the Maven project.

In addition to that, I also like how Eclipse handles Maven projects (and especially multi-module Maven projects) in general. As mentioned before, Eclipse can automatically link Maven projects in the same workspace if they depend on each other for example.

Enterprise features

At the beginning, I mentioned that it's important to think about the IntelliJ Edition you want to compare Eclipse to. Regarding that, many of the features that would only be available with IntelliJ's paid version are available for free (and are Open Source) with the Eclipse IDE.

No AI crap forced upon me

With Eclipse, there is no AI shoved into my face without me wanting it. Of course, I could install a plugin if I really wanted to use some AI tool but Eclipse doesn't try to convince me into vibe coding. I don't want AI "helping" me with developing software and I don't want an IDE trying to sell me AI features.

Other differences

In addition to how these two IDEs are different on their own, I also want to talk about some other important differences that you may not directly see within the applications.

While Eclipse had some issues with maintenance and was slow with adding features at some point in the past, the Eclipse IDE improved a lot in recent years (you can take a look at the recent New and Noteworthy pages if you want to).

FOSS

The Eclipse IDE is fully Free and Open Source software and it is vendor-neutral. There isn't a company who might ensh*ttify it and we all can modify the code of any part of Eclipse to our liking.

While Intellij's Community Edition is mostly Open Source, everything is Open Source with Eclipse (except maybe some third-party tools/plugins). If I install an official Eclipse package, everything in it is Open Source. And this isn't just about the code being available under an Open Source license, the entire development of the Eclipse IDE happens transparently in public. This also allows other projects to benefit from the Eclipse IDE. For example, the Java tooling of Visual Studio Code is based on Eclipse's JDT-Core.

In general, I think it's better to use Open Source software where possible.

It being Open Source also allows anyone (with the necessary skill) to fix bugs or build their own features and contribute them back such that everyone benefits from it. I myself contributed some things that I wanted to have available.

The Eclipse IDE is not just an Open Source project, it is a Community-oriented meritocracy. They are very open to contributions from anyone.

Some things where IntelliJ is better

Now that I told you about some reasons why I personally prefer Eclipse, there are also a few things where IntelliJ is better.

Marketing

The biggest thing where IntelliJ does better is marketing (even though it probably won't affect your experience developing software much). As a big company, JetBrains can spend quite a lot of resources on marketing whereas there isn't really any marketing for the Eclipse IDE (except maybe some people trying to help people contribute but I don't think that counts).

Complexity and beginner-friendlyness

Due to Eclipse being really powerful with a lot of features and options added over time, Eclipse also comes with a lot of complexity. While IntelliJ is complex in many ways as well, it is better at "hiding" the complexity in a way that it is easier to work with out-of-the-box. This includes things like the (default) layout where Eclipse just shows you a lot of things while IntelliJ is typically "cleaner" as well as the preferences where Eclipse can be pretty overwhelming. I also feel like there was more work put into making IntelliJ beginner-friendly (probably partly due to marketing reasons) whereas Eclipse is built by people using it adding whatever they consider is useful.

"UI clutter"

In my experience, many people consider Eclipse's UI to be "cluttered" (which is also related to the point of "complexity").

Disclaimer

I have contributed to the Eclipse IDE in the past (mainly the Java tooling) and I will probably continue to do so in the future. I am (at least at the time of writing this) not an Eclipse Committer. I am not paid to work on anything Eclipse related (at least at the time of writing this) but I have interest in making sure Eclipse is as good as possible as I am using it and as I would like to continue using it. I have previously written a similar version of this here as people sometimes asked me why I prefer Eclipse over IntelliJ.

Q: Difference between Use Case, Action, and Application Service in DDD A:

In Domain-Driven Design (DDD), an Application Service (e.g. ProductMaintenanceService) is the technical expression of one or more Use Cases. (Typically it contains / implements multiple use cases, e.g. registerProduct, modifyProduct, and deleteProduct). Whereas an Action (say changeProductPrice) is one of the technical executions of the modifyProduct use case

DDD's primary strategic value lies in improving communication and aligning software development with business needs by creating a "Ubiquitous" Language between users and developers.

Q: Double quotes vs asterisk filename expansion in Bash A:

The problem here is not with cp, but with for, because by default it splits the output of your subshell by words, not by directory names.

A lazy workaround is to use while instead and process the list of directories line by line like this:

find . -type d -name '*foo' | while read dir; do cp "$dir"/* "$(echo $dir | sed 's_foo__g')" ; done

This should fix your problem with spaces, but this is by no means a foolproof solution.

See Charles Duffy's answer for a more accurate solution.

Q: Assumption with double quotes, single quotes and no quotes A:

Short answer: Yes

These assumptions are basically true, always!

variable='2010-09-08 12:34:56'
vname=variable
date -d "$variable" +%s
1283942096

date -d "${!vname}" +%s
1283942096

date -d $variable +%s
date: extra operand '+%s'
Try 'date --help' for more information.

date -d '$variable' +%s
date: invalid date '$variable'

date -d ${!vname} +%s
date: extra operand '+%s'
Try 'date --help' for more information.

But

  1. Some commands, like xargs, work precisely about expansion and parameter distribution.

     echo "$variable" | xargs date +%s -d
 date: extra operand '12:34:56'
 Try 'date --help' for more information.

    You have to use -0 arg to xargs:

     echo "$variable" | xargs -0 date +%s -d
 1283942096

  2. Built-in commands could use arguments differently, especially eval:

     cmd='printf "%s\n" $(date -d "$variable" +%c)'
 eval $cmd
 Wed
 Sep
 8
 12:34:56
 2010

 cmd='printf "%s\n" "$(date -d "$variable" +%c)"'
 eval "$cmd"
 Wed Sep  8 12:34:56 2010

 eval $cmd
 Wed Sep  8 12:34:56 2010

 bash -c "$cmd"
 Mon May 16 00:00:00 2016

 bash -c $cmd
 printf: usage: printf [-v var] format [arguments]

  3. The syntax of funny things under Bash are not limited to "..", '..', and ${}

    • $'...' lets you print special characters, but it doesn't expand variables:

        echo $'This\tis\ta string containing ${variable}'
  This    is    a string containing ${variable}

    • Backticks: For compatibility, backticks are always supported. If not very readable, you may see this in some scripts:

        echo `date +%c -d "${!vname}"`
  Wed Sep 8 12:34:56 2010

    • The syntax $"..." could be used for localization:

        export TEXTDOMAIN=bash
  export LANG=fr_CH.utf-8
  echo $"Running"
  En cours d'exécution

And care about no quotes!

Where you said:

echo * # Globbing always done.
echo $variable; # Variable expansion is always done
echo $(command) # Command expansion is always done

Try this:

xx='/t*p/.'
echo '$xx'   # No expansion
$xx
echo "$xx"   # Variable expansion
/t*p/.
echo $xx     # Variable and globbing expansion
/tmp/.

Where globbing expansion is done after variable expansion.
